MANILA, Philippines — It is becoming harder for internet service providers (ISPs) to retain low-income subscribers, who are feeling the pain of the double whammy of rising prices and a weak peso.
While Converge ICT Solutions Inc. has grown its subscriber base to 3.1 million to date, the ISP is struggling to acquire and retain consumers in its low-cost product Surf2Sawa.
Converge chief operations officer Benjamin Azada said the impact of a declining peso and hot inflation is hitting the provider’s low-income subscribers.
Azada said, however, that its flagship service FiberX is picking up steady demand. FiberX caters to middle-income families, as its price ranges between P1,349 and P2,599 monthly.
On the other hand, Converge created Surf2Sawa to reach low-income families, or those who prefer to buy monthly subscriptions in sachets. Surf2Sawa offers 30-day broadband for just P700.
Azada said even though Surf2Sawa is already Converge’s cheapest package, demand for it goes up and down depending on the economic situation.
For instance, in the third quarter, inflation stayed above the six-percent level, and even climbed to 7.2 percent in September, compelling consumers to keep their spending in check.
Still, Azada is optimistic about Surf2Sawa’s prospects in this economic landscape, especially as Converge is a pioneer in low-cost broadband.
Further, Converge is working toward cutting the price of broadband further, as it hopes to reach the affordability threshold for connectivity. The ISP is exploring a new product that would allow it to offer fiber broadband for only P500 a month, even cheaper than Surf2Sawa.
The International Telecommunication Union has set an affordability threshold for connectivity at two percent of gross national income (GNI) per capita. However, a broadband connection in the Philippines currently costs four percent of GNI per capita, according to Opensignal.
Converge CEO and co-founder Dennis Anthony Uy said the ISP would keep on putting out fresh products to serve different markets and varying needs across the archipelago.
He also underscored the importance of rolling out network assets in as many areas as possible to achieve economies of scale in a time when costs are rising.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine economy slowed even further in the third quarter of 2026, posting its weakest growth since 2009, excluding the pandemic years.
Gross domestic product (GDP), the common measure of the economy based on the value of goods and services produced locally, expanded by 2.1% year-on-year in Q3 2026, the Philippine Statistics Authority said on Monday, November 9.
That is even lower than the revised 2.4% growth recorded in Q2 2026, and also below the revised 4% posted in Q3 2025.
This also marks the fifth consecutive quarter of slowing growth, from 5.5% in Q2 2025 to 4% in Q3 2025, 3% in Q4 2025, 2.8% in Q1 2026, and 2.4% in Q2 2026.
Growth for the first nine months of 2026 stood at 2.5%. That means the latest GDP figure leaves even less room for the government as it faces a difficult climb toward its already slashed full-year growth target of 3.5% to 4.5%.
Balisacan acknowledged that the economy would have to grow by about 6.3% in the fourth quarter just to reach the lower end of the target, which he described as “very, very challenging.”
GDP growth for the quarter also turned out to be worse than most economists expected. For instance, ahead of the release, Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. warned that private construction continued to weaken, while consumers were still hesitant to spend for discretionary goods as inflation squeezed their wallets. Still, Neri had expected a modest uptick to 3.2%, supported by stronger electronics support and government spending.
In its midyear Philippines Economic Update, the World Bank projected economic growth of 3.7% for 2026, with fixed investment expected to contract by 0.5% and private consumption growth slowing to 3.5%. The bank maintained its overall GDP forecast in October.
Meanwhile, the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office cut its growth forecast for 2026 to only 3.3%.
Department of Economy, Planning, and Development Secretary Arsenio Balisacan attributed the continued slowdown to a multitude of factors, including high food and energy prices, disruptions to agriculture caused by bad weather, and weak investment.
Household spending, which has traditionally driven the Philippine economy, slowed further to 2.4% in Q3 from 2.9% in Q2. Spending on transportation also shrank by 5.3%, while food and non-alcoholic beverage consuption, which accounts for nearly a third of household spending, grew by just 1.6%.
With inflation reaching 7.8% in October, Balisacan warned that he doesn’t “expect the consumer spending to rebound strongly soon” because there are still “lag effects of that inflation,” adding that inflation for November will likely “continue to be challenged.”
Agriculture, which accounts for around 7% of the Philippine economy, contracted by 4.8%, with palay and corn output plunging by 17.8% and 17.4%, respectively. Fishing and aquaculture also declined by 8.5%.
The construction industry, meanwhile, contracted by 4%. On the investment side, construction spending fell by 3.5%, dragged down by a 15.1% decline in government construction, while spending by corporations and households barely grew.
“Agencies, especially those on the ground, are a bit cautious about acting on projects, especially those that are already ongoing,” Balisacan said, acknowledging that officials were concerned about becoming involved in “infrastructure scandals.” (READ: Flood control corruption cleanup spooks investors, drags PH growth – World Bank)

CEBU, Philippines — Philippine economic growth slowed further in the third quarter to its weakest expansion in more than five years, casting doubt on the government’s full-year growth target.
In a press conference, National Statistician Dennis Mapa said the country’s gross domestic product grew by just 2.1 percent in the third quarter, slower than the previous quarter’s GDP growth of 2.4 percent and the four percent expansion in the third quarter last year.
He described the third quarter growth as the “slowest since the first quarter of 2021 during the pandemic period,” when the economy contracted by 3.8 percent.
Excluding the pandemic, he said the third-quarter GDP print was the lowest since the fourth quarter of 2009, when the growth rate was only 1.8 percent.
The latest GDP result brought average growth from the first to the third quarter to 2.5 percent, making the government’s full-year growth target difficult to achieve.
Department of Economy, Planning and Development Secretary Arsenio Balisacan attributed the weak growth performance to high food and energy prices that dampened consumption, lowered agricultural output and subdued investment amid tighter financing conditions.
Household spending growth slowed to 2.4 percent in the third quarter from the previous quarter’s 2.9 percent amid higher fuel prices stemming from the Middle East conflict that also pushed up transport, electricity and production costs.
The agriculture sector also contributed to the weak growth, contracting by 4.8 percent in the third quarter and reversing the previous quarter’s 2.9 percent growth as heavy rains disrupted farm production.
Growth was also dragged down by public construction, which declined for the sixth consecutive quarter, contracting by 15.1 percent compared to the previous quarter’s 33.4 percent.
Balisacan said weather disruptions and delays in project validation and payments affected the delivery of government infrastructure projects.
“Governance concerns and uncertainty also weighed on confidence,” he said.
Gross capital formation or investment contracted by 0.2 percent in the third quarter, but eased from the 8.8 percent decline in the previous quarter.
Despite the slower growth in the third quarter, Balisacan said this does not signal that the economy is entering stagflation. He also said it is best to wait for full-year data and broader economic indicators to get a clearer picture.
Stagflation is a situation marked by low economic growth, high inflation and high unemployment.
To reach the lower end of the government’s growth target for this year, Balisacan said that economic growth in the fourth quarter should reach about 6.3 percent.
“The target of 3.5 to 4.5 percent is very, very challenging at this point given the current environment, but we are hoping, and I would like to believe that the fourth quarter performance will be better,” he said.
If the economy posts at least three percent growth this year, he said it would already be a remarkable achievement given the performance in the first three quarters.
The economy needs to grow by around four to 4.5 percent in the fourth quarter for full-year 2026 growth to reach three percent.
Balisacan said the slower contraction in investment in the third quarter could be a starting point for recovery.

related.text:
INCREASE. Another round of fuel price adjustments takes effect in Manila, on April 7, 2026.
MANILA, Philippines – Fuel prices are set for a bigtime rollback starting Tuesday, November 10.
The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the following permitted price adjustments for November 10 to 16:
Gasoline – rollback of at least P16.80 per liter
Diesel – rollback of at least P4.10 per liter
Kerosene – rollback of at least P3.70 per liter
Last week, gasoline prices saw a hike of as much as P3.50 per liter, while diesel and kerosene prices fell by at least P1 and P1.90 per liter, respectively.
International oil prices fell as hope rekindled for the easing of tensions between the United States and Iran following the US midterm elections. A possible de-escalation of the conflict could allow more Middle Eastern oil to reach global markets, improving the strained supply.
Local pump prices remain substantially higher than before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, common Metro Manila prices stood at P56 per liter for RON95 gasoline, P54.70 for RON91, P55 for diesel, and P83.47 for kerosene.
The Philippines imports much of its petroleum requirements as finished products, making domestic prices vulnerable to changes in regional fuel markets, freight costs, and foreign exchange rates.
Meanwhile, excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene remain suspended under Executive Order No. 125, issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in September. The relief does not cover gasoline or diesel. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines — Motorists are in for some relief as major pump price rollbacks take effect across the board today, with gasoline prices dropping by at least P16.80 per liter.
Diesel and kerosene prices will also see substantial reductions, with minimum rollbacks of P4.10 and P3.70 per liter, respectively.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin attributed the steep price cuts to declining global crude oil prices amid easing tensions between the United States and Iran.
The rollback also reflects market reactions to the US midterm elections, where sweeping Democratic party victories against President Donald Trump’s Republican Party eased fears of a further escalation of the Iran war.
“What’s happening in other countries likely affects international fuel prices and hence, petroleum prices here in the Philippines are affected,” Garin told a media briefing yesterday.
She, however, said it could take time before domestic pump prices return to pre-war levels, noting the peso’s depreciation against the dollar is adding upward pressure on fuel costs.
As a net oil importer, the Philippines remains vulnerable to fluctuations in global oil prices, particularly amid persistent geopolitical uncertainties.
Energy Undersecretary Alessandro Sales, meanwhile, said state-run Philippine National Oil Co. remains committed to its plan to build fuel storage facilities with a combined capacity of up to one million barrels.
The first storage tank with a capacity of 180,000 barrels is targeted for completion before the end of 2027.
